description:
'''Southern hip-hop''' or '''Southern rap''', also known colloquially as '''Dirty South''' music, is [[hip-hop music]] from the [[Southern United States]]. As hip-hop spread beyond its origins in [[New York City]], several Southern cities began developing their own hip-hop scenes in the 1980s; in particular, [[Atlanta]], [[Houston]], [[New Orleans]], [[Miami]], and [[Memphis, Tennessee|Memphis]] have become regional hip-hop hubs. Typical characteristics of the Southern hip-hop sound include a focus on bass-heavy beats; relatively little use of [[sampling (music)|sampling]], in favor of live or synthesized instrumentation; and a decreased emphasis on lyrical complexity, instead incorporating other vocal styles such as [[Call and response (music)|call-and-response]] chants or heavily processed singing. Much Southern hip-hop is targeted toward environments like nightclubs, and popular dances such as [[twerking]] have emerged in close connection with the genre. Southern hip-hop also encompasses a wide range of subgenres, including [[trap music|trap]], [[crunk]], and [[bounce music|bounce]], among others.

The earliest Southern hip-hop act to attain national attention was Miami's [[2 Live Crew]], who were at the forefront of the [[Miami bass]] scene in the late 1980s and who won a highly publicized legal battle against officials seeking to criminalize their work as obscene. Houston's [[Geto Boys]] followed around 1990, with a [[hardcore hip-hop]] style that also courted controversy. As the 1990s progressed, [[Outkast]] achieved both critical and commercial success; the group's defiant response to being booed at the [[1995 Source Awards]] has become one of the genre's most highly discussed incidents. Meanwhile in New Orleans, two independent record labels—[[No Limit Records|No Limit]] and [[Cash Money Records|Cash Money]]—signed major distribution deals that led their artists to national prominence in the decade's later years.

In the 2000s, a series of popular hip-hop subgenres emerged from Atlanta. Crunk was widespread in the early part of the decade, owing to the work of [[Lil Jon]] in particular, while the decade's second half saw the ascent of trap artists like [[T.I.]], [[Jeezy]], and [[Gucci Mane]]. In Houston, the [[chopped and screwed]] style—originally pioneered by [[DJ Screw]]—enjoyed a period of national success around 2005, fueled by the [[Swishahouse]] label. As trap evolved in the 2010s, artists like [[Lex Luger (music producer)|Lex Luger]] helped spread trap-influenced production into other genres like pop, while rappers like [[Future (rapper)|Future]] adapted it into [[mumble rap]]. During this period, Southern rappers like [[Soulja Boy]] and the [[Raider Klan]] capitalized on the Internet to further their styles and careers.

In addition to its musical style, Southern hip-hop has been regarded as distinctive for local slang terms like "trill" and "[[bling-bling]]", which have been extensively used and popularized within the genre. Southern hip-hop music is also commonly associated with the wearing of [[grill (jewelry)|grill]]s, an emphasis on cars, and the consumption of the drug [[lean (drug)|lean]].
